items.name: Readability
items.evidence: All the code is ad-hoc inline `python3 -c` one-liners with single-letter names throughout: `d=open('main.db-wal','rb').read()`, `c=sqlite3.connect(...)`, `r=[dict(id=a,name=b,value=v) ...]`. There are no comments and no named script.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: No decrypt or extract script was kept, which ignores the convention asking for a short, re-runnable recovery. The only results are a JSON file written by a one-liner and a deleted `main.db-wal`. Scratch work went to /tmp/w and /tmp/v.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The XOR key `0x42` is hardcoded in code with no check that the decrypted magic is 0x377f0682/3. There is no error handling. A chained command opened /app/main.db read-write with the encrypted WAL, and SQLite discarded the WAL.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The agent derived key 0x42 from the WAL header (`75 3d 44 c0` -> `37 7f 06 82`), XORed the whole file, and let SQLite replay the WAL on a copy. It checked the result with `count(*)` = 11. It did not run integrity_check, a minor gap.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: In step [2], `main.db` was opened read-write while the WAL was still encrypted, and SQLite deleted `main.db-wal`. The backup `cp main.db-wal /tmp/wal.orig.bak` only ran in step [3], after the file was gone. The agent admits there was no backup of the original.
